title: Jaishankar Meets Ghana's Mahama as Accra Courts Indian Pharma Investment
excerpt: Opening a five-day tour of Ghana, Côte d'Ivoire and Ethiopia, the foreign minister's Accra visit centred on pharmaceuticals, agriculture and industrialisation — with Mahama pitching a rebounding economy to Indian investors.
body:
• External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar met Ghana's President John Dramani Mahama at the Presidency in Accra on Tuesday, opening a five-day tour of Ghana, Côte d'Ivoire and Ethiopia.
  • Mahama used the meeting to pitch Ghana as "open for business," courting Indian investment in pharmaceutical and vaccine manufacturing under his government's Accra Reset initiative for African health sovereignty.
  • "Ghana's economy is doing well. It is stable. Inflation is low, interest rates are going down, and the currency is holding its own," Mahama said. "I think that this is the best time to invest." FDI is projected to surpass $3 billion in 2026, up from $2.6 billion in 2025.
  • The visit builds on PM Modi's historic state visit to Ghana in 2025; talks will cover pharma, agricultural mechanisation, industrialisation, job creation, scholarships and IT partnerships.

External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar met Ghana's President John Dramani Mahama in Accra on Tuesday, launching a five-day Africa tour aimed at deepening India's partnerships across West and East Africa. The Ghana leg, running October 6–7, is the first stop before Jaishankar travels to Côte d'Ivoire and Ethiopia.

"Open for business"

During a courtesy call at the Presidency, Mahama declared Ghana "open for business," inviting Indian companies to capitalise on expanding opportunities in the country's pharmaceutical and vaccine manufacturing sectors. He pledged continued policy reforms under the government's #ResettingGhana agenda and the Accra Reset initiative, aimed at securing health sovereignty across Africa.

"Ghana's economy is doing well. It is stable. Inflation is low, interest rates are going down, and the currency is holding its own," Mahama said. "I think that this is the best time to invest."

To underscore the recovery, the president said foreign direct investment into Ghana rose from $2.6 billion in 2025, with projections showing it could surpass $3 billion in 2026. On healthcare, he pointed to the partnership between Atlantic Life Sciences and indigenous firm KinaPharma as a working model for localising vaccine production — "part of our effort to localise vaccine production, but there is still substantial room for expansion," he said.

The agenda

Ghana's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which invited Jaishankar at the behest of Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, described the visit as "historic" — an opportunity to "renew their inseparable bond of solidarity and shared values." Talks will advance pharmaceutical development within Mahama's Accra Reset philosophy, deepen agricultural cooperation in mechanisation and value addition, support the president's industrialisation and job-creation agenda, and expand scholarships and IT partnerships.

India is already a leading supplier of generic medicines to West Africa, making the pharma partnership a natural area for deeper engagement. In July, the two countries also discussed strengthening maritime and port-sector cooperation, with India's High Commissioner-designate to Ghana, Surinder Bhagat, meeting the Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority.

"Ghana's economy is doing well. It is stable. Inflation is low, interest rates are going down, and the currency is holding its own. I think that this is the best time to invest."

— John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana

India's Africa play

The External Affairs Ministry framed the visit as a reflection of "India's commitment to deepen its partnership with Africa" and its solidarity with the Global South. The tour builds on the historic state visit of Prime Minister Narendra Modi to Ghana in 2025, and follows a pattern of accelerating high-level engagement — including India's championing of the African Union's permanent G20 membership during its 2023 presidency.

During his transit through Addis Ababa, Jaishankar also met Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey. In Ethiopia, he will chair the Regional Heads of Mission conference, where discussions will cover the full range of bilateral ties — trade and economic cooperation, development partnership, capacity building and people-to-people links — alongside regional and global issues of mutual interest.

Diaspora angle

Ghana hosts a long-standing Indian business community, and the pharma-and-vaccines pitch lands directly in its lap: Indian firms are already among the biggest suppliers of affordable medicines to West Africa. If Mahama's Accra Reset translates into real manufacturing partnerships, it could open a new chapter for Indian pharmaceutical investment on the continent — and for the diaspora entrepreneurs positioned to build it.

What's next

After Accra, Jaishankar heads to Côte d'Ivoire and then Ethiopia, where the Heads of Mission conference will set the tone for India's Africa diplomacy in the coming year. Watch for concrete announcements on pharma manufacturing partnerships and development projects — the test of whether the "open for business" pitch converts into signed deals.
